blocks.text: 1.4.1 Polar Coordinate System of a Complex Number

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text: Kitab ne is heading ka number 1.4.1 likha hai, jo woh pehle hi "Properties of Cube Roots of Unity" (kitab ka page 12) ke liye use kar chuki hai. Hum ne number kitab jaisa rakha hai taa ke aap isay kitab mein dhoond saken; ghalti sirf numbering mein hai, maths theek hai.

Is sabaq mein hum seekhenge ke kisi complex number ko polar form mein kaise likhte hain. Pichle topic mein aap ne dekha tha ke kisi point ko "kitni door aur kis taraf" se bataya ja sakta hai. Aur is se pehle Argand diagram mein aap ne complex number \(z = x + iy\) ko point \((x, y)\) bana kar plot kiya tha, aur modulus \(|z|\) ko origin se us point ka faasla samjha tha. Ab hum yeh dono baatein jod denge: complex number ko uske distance aur angle ki zabaan mein likhenge.

Saath wali figure dekhiye. Complex number \(z = x + iy\) ko Argand plane mein point \(A\) dikhaya gaya hai. \(O\) ko \(A\) se milaiye, aur \(A\) se \(x\)-axis par perpendicular (amood, seedhi khadi line) \(AM\) giraaiye. Ab ek right triangle \(OMA\) ban gaya. Is ka hypotenuse (sab se lamba bazu, right angle ke saamne) \(OA = r\) hai, base \(OM = x\) hai, perpendicular \(AM = y\) hai, aur \(O\) par angle \(\theta\) hai.
Ab trigonometry ki bunyaadi definitions yaad kijiye: \(\cos\) = base/hypotenuse aur \(\sin\) = perpendicular/hypotenuse. Is liye
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{r},\quad \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{r}\]
Dono taraf \(r\) se multiply karne par
\[x = r\cos\theta \quad\text{aur}\quad y = r\sin\theta\]
Yahan \(r = |z|\) modulus hai (origin se point ka faasla), aur \(\theta\) ko \(z\) ka argument kehte hain (yaani woh angle jo \(OA\) positive \(x\)-axis ke saath banata hai).

blocks.alt: Axes x and y with origin O. A segment from O to the point A(r, θ), labelled square root of (x squared + y squared), makes angle θ with the x-axis. A vertical segment from A meets the x-axis at M; MA is marked y = r sin θ and OM is marked x = r cos θ.
blocks.caption: Figure: the complex number z = x + iy as the point A(r, θ); x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
Ab \(x\) aur \(y\) ki jagah yeh values \(z = x + iy\) mein rakh dijiye:
\[x + iy = r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta \quad \text{(i)}\]
\(r\) common nikaalne par \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), jahan
\[r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\]
\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}\quad (x \ne 0)\]
\(r\) wala formula Pythagoras theorem se aata hai (hypotenuse\(^2\) = base\(^2\) + perpendicular\(^2\)), aur \(\theta\) wala formula \(\tan\theta = y/x\) se. Equation (i) ko complex number \(z\) ki polar form kehte hain.

blocks.text_alt: z equals r times open bracket cos theta plus i sin theta close bracket

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Polar form ki zaroorat kyun hai? Rectangular form \(x + iy\) batati hai "kitna right aur kitna upar". Polar form batati hai "origin se kitni door aur kis direction mein". Dono ek hi number ke do naam hain, jaise ek hi ghar ka pata "gali number 3, makaan number 5" bhi ho sakta hai aur "chowk se 200 metre, masjid ki taraf" bhi.
Asal faida aage aayega: 1.3.3 mein aap dekhenge ke polar form mein complex numbers ko multiply aur divide karna bohat aasan hai: distances ko multiply kijiye aur angles ko jama kijiye. Rectangular form mein yahi kaam lamba aur thakaane wala hai.
Ek form se doosri mein jaane ke formule:
• polar se rectangular: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\).
• rectangular se polar: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), aur \(\theta\) ko \(\tan\theta = y/x\) se nikaaliye, lekin sahi quadrant dekh kar (is ki tafseel neeche Principal Argument mein hai).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Hum \(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta = \operatorname{cis}\theta\) likh sakte hain, is liye polar form ko \(z = r\operatorname{cis}\theta\) bhi likhte hain.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"cis" koi naya function nahi, sirf chhota naam (short form) hai: c se cos, i se \(i\), s se sin. Jahan bhi \(\operatorname{cis}\theta\) dekhein, foran zehan mein \(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta\) padhiye.
Ab kitab ki misaal dekhte hain. Is mein hum wahi steps follow karenge jo upar formula banate waqt kiye: parts barabar karna, \(r\) nikaalna, \(\theta\) nikaalna.

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: Express the complex number \(1 + i\sqrt{3}\) in polar form.
steps:
Given: \(z = 1 + i\sqrt{3}\). Is ka real part \(x = 1\) aur imaginary part \(y = \sqrt{3}\) hai.
Find karna hai: \(r\) aur \(\theta\), taa ke \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\) likh saken.
Tareeqa: sab se pehle hum yeh samajhte hain ke humein find kya karna hai: sirf do cheezein, distance \(r\) aur angle \(\theta\). Polar form \(r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta\) ko given number ke saath barabar rakhenge. Phir square kar ke jama karne se \(r\) milega, divide karne se \(\tan\theta\) milega, aur aakhir mein \(x\) aur \(y\) ke signs dekh kar quadrant pakka karenge.

Step I: real aur imaginary parts barabar kijiye
\[r\cos\theta = 1 \quad \text{(1)}\]
\[r\sin\theta = \sqrt{3} \quad \text{(2)}\]
Kyun: \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta\). Do complex numbers tab barabar hote hain jab un ke real parts barabar hon aur imaginary parts barabar hon (yeh rule hum 1.2 Equality mein parh chuke hain). Is liye real part \(1\) ko \(r\cos\theta\) ke barabar rakha, aur imaginary part \(\sqrt{3}\) ko \(r\sin\theta\) ke barabar.
Dhyan dein: imaginary part ke saath hamesha \(\sin\) aata hai. Kitab mein yahan doosri equation mein bhi \(\cos\) chhap gaya hai; yeh printing ki ghalti hai (neeche "Kitab ki ghalti" dekhiye).

Step II: r nikaliye
(1) aur (2) dono ko square kar ke jama kijiye:
\[r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta = 1 + 3\]
\[r^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = 4\]
\[r^2 = 4\]
\[r = 2\]
Kyun: square kar ke jama karne ka faida yeh hai ke \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) wali identity se \(\theta\) bilkul khatam ho jata hai aur sirf \(r\) bachta hai. \(r^2 = 4\) se \(r = \pm 2\) nikalta hai, lekin hum \(r = 2\) lete hain, \(-2\) nahi, kyun ke \(r = |z|\) faasla (distance) hai, aur faasla kabhi negative nahi hota.
Kitab yahi baat seedha \(r^2 = 1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2\) likh kar karti hai; yeh asal mein \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) wala formula hi hai.

Step III: θ nikaliye
(2) ko (1) se divide kijiye:
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1} = \sqrt{3}\]
\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = 60^{\circ}\]
Kyun: divide karne se \(r\) cancel ho jata hai, kyun ke \(\dfrac{r\sin\theta}{r\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\). Ab ruk kar quadrant check kijiye: \(x = 1 > 0\) aur \(y = \sqrt{3} > 0\), dono positive, is liye point first quadrant mein hai. First quadrant mein \(\tan^{-1}\) seedha sahi angle de deta hai. Table se: \(60^{\circ} = \pi/3\).

Step IV: polar form likhiye
\[1 + i\sqrt{3} = 2\cos 60^{\circ} + i\,2\sin 60^{\circ}\]
\[= 2(\cos 60^{\circ} + i\sin 60^{\circ})\]
\[= 2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
Kyun: \(r = 2\) aur \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\) ko \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\) mein rakh diya, aur 2 ko common nikaal liya. Aakhri line mein wahi jawab "cis" notation mein likha hai.

Tasdeeq: jawab ko wapas rectangular form mein badal kar dekhiye
\[2\cos 60^{\circ} = 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\]
\[2\sin 60^{\circ} = 2 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}\]
Is liye \(2(\cos 60^{\circ} + i\sin 60^{\circ}) = 1 + i\sqrt{3}\). Wahi number wapas mil gaya, matlab jawab sahi hai. Exam mein bhi yeh do line ki tasdeeq zaroor kar liya kijiye.

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text: Example 12 ke Step I mein kitab "Put \(r\cos\theta = 1\) and \(r\cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\)" chhaapti hai. Doosri equation \(r\sin\theta = \sqrt{3}\) honi chahiye, kyun ke \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\) ka imaginary part \(r\sin\theta\) hai. Kitab ka baaqi hal (\(r = 2\), \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\)) bilkul sahi hai; humne upar sahi equation likhi hai.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
• Agar \(x = 0,\ y > 0\) ho to \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
• Agar \(x = 0,\ y < 0\) ho to \(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
• Agar \(x = 0,\ y = 0\) ho to \(\theta\) undefined hai.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Kitab ne yeh Note kyun diya? Ruk kar sochiye: \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(y/x)\) mein hum \(y\) ko \(x\) se divide karte hain. Agar \(x = 0\) ho to zero se divide karna padega, jo mumkin nahi. Is liye aisi soorat mein formula chhod kar angle seedha figure se parhte hain:
• Positive imaginary axis par point (misaal ke taur par \(2i\)) seedha upar ki taraf hai, is liye angle \(\pi/2\), yaani \(90^{\circ}\).
• Negative imaginary axis par point (misaal ke taur par \(-3i\)) seedha neeche ki taraf hai, is liye angle \(-\pi/2\).
• Number \(0\) to khud pole hai. Wahan se kisi taraf jaana hi nahi, is liye us ki koi direction nahi, aur koi argument bhi nahi. Is ko "undefined" kehte hain.

Pichle topic mein humne dekha tha ke ek point ke beshumaar angles ho sakte hain, kyun ke \(2\pi\) ka poora chakkar laga kar hum wapas usi direction mein aa jaate hain. Exam mein sab students ek hi jawab dein, is ke liye ek standard angle chuna jata hai. Isay principal argument kehte hain.
Principal Argument: complex number \(z = a + bi\) ka principal argument \(\theta\) woh angle hai jo Argand plane mein positive real axis aur point \((a, b)\) ko origin se milane wali line ke darmiyan banta hai. Kitab isay aise likhti hai:
\[\arg z = \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\]
Isay \(\arg\) se denote karte hain. Yeh argument ki ek hi, khaas value hai, jo is standard range (had) mein chuni jaati hai:
\[\arg z \in (-\pi, \pi]\]
Is range ka matlab hai: \(-\pi\) se bara aur \(\pi\) ke barabar ya us se chhota.

blocks.title: Aam ghalti
blocks.text:
Bohat se students yahan ghalti karte hain: woh sirf calculator par \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) daba kar angle likh dete hain. Masla yeh hai ke calculator ka \(\tan^{-1}\) hamesha \(-\pi/2\) aur \(\pi/2\) ke darmiyan ka angle deta hai. Is liye yeh sirf tab sahi hai jab \(a > 0\) ho (point imaginary axis ke daayen taraf ho).
Misaal: \(z = -1 - i\). Yahan \(b/a = 1\) aur \(\tan^{-1} 1 = \pi/4\). Lekin \(-1 - i\) third quadrant mein hai, jab ke \(\pi/4\) first quadrant ki taraf ishara karta hai. Sahi principal argument \(-3\pi/4\) hai.
Wajah: \(\dfrac{-1}{-1}\) aur \(\dfrac{1}{1}\) dono ek hi number hain, is liye \(b/a\) ko \(a\) aur \(b\) ke signs "bhool" jaate hain. Hal: hamesha pehle signs dekh kar quadrant pehchaaniye, phir angle nikaaliye.

Principal argument sahi nikaalne ka tareeqa (hamara method, teen qadam):
1. \(a\) aur \(b\) ke signs dekh kar faisla kijiye ke \(z\) kis quadrant (ya kis axis) par hai. Ek chhota sa rough sketch bohat madad karta hai.
2. Reference angle \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left|\dfrac{b}{a}\right|\) nikaaliye. Absolute value lene se yeh hamesha \(0\) aur \(\pi/2\) ke darmiyan ka acute (chhota) angle hoga, signs ki fikr ke baghair.
3. Neeche wali table se quadrant ke mutabiq \(\theta\) likhiye, jo \((-\pi, \pi]\) mein ho.
Table ka mantiq (logic) samajh lijiye, ratne ki zaroorat nahi rahegi: upar wale quadrants (I, II) mein angle positive hai aur neeche wale (III, IV) mein negative. Quadrant II mein hum \(\pi\) se \(\alpha\) peeche aate hain; Quadrant III mein wahi angle neeche ki taraf, is liye minus.

blocks.caption: Teaching table (hamari taraf se): z = a + bi ka principal argument, jahan α = tan⁻¹|b/a|

blocks.title: Hamari taraf se misaalein
blocks.text:
Table ke saath practice kijiye (yeh hamari misaalein hain, kitab ki nahi):
• \(z = -1 + i\): \(a < 0, b > 0\), Quadrant II. \(\alpha = \tan^{-1} 1 = \pi/4\), is liye \(\arg z = \pi - \pi/4 = 3\pi/4\).
• \(z = -1 - i\): Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \pi/4\), is liye \(\arg z = -(\pi - \pi/4) = -3\pi/4\).
• \(z = 1 - i\): Quadrant IV, \(\alpha = \pi/4\), is liye \(\arg z = -\pi/4\).
• \(z = -\sqrt{3} - i\): Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}(1/\sqrt{3}) = \pi/6\), is liye \(\arg z = -5\pi/6\).
• \(z = -4\): negative real axis, \(\arg z = \pi\).
Khud sochiye: \(z = \sqrt{3} - i\) ka principal argument kya hoga? (Quadrant IV, \(\alpha = \pi/6\), jawab \(-\pi/6\).)

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
Range \((-\pi, \pi]\) hi kyun? Kisi bhi argument mein poora chakkar \(2\pi\) jama ya tafreeq karne se point apni jagah se nahi hilta, is liye \(z\) ke beshumaar arguments hote hain: \(\theta + 2k\pi\) (\(k\) koi bhi integer). Range \((-\pi, \pi]\) ki lambai theek \(2\pi\) hai, is liye is mein in mein se sirf ek hi value aati hai.
\(\pi\) range mein shaamil hai (yeh negative real axis ki direction hai) aur \(-\pi\) shaamil nahi, taa ke negative real axis ko sirf ek hi value mile. Isi liye bracket ek taraf gol "(" aur doosri taraf chakor "]" hai.
Real axis se upar wale points ke principal arguments positive (\(0\) se \(\pi\)) hote hain, aur neeche wale points ke negative (\(0\) se \(-\pi\)).

blocks.title: Yaad rakhne wali baatein
blocks.text:
• \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), is liye \(z = x + iy = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).
• \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) modulus hai (hamesha \(\ge 0\)); \(\theta\) \(z\) ka ek argument hai.
• Polar form banane ka tareeqa: parts barabar kijiye, square kar ke jama kar ke \(r\), divide kar ke \(\tan\theta\), phir quadrant check.
• Imaginary axis par: \(\theta = \pi/2\) (upar) ya \(-\pi/2\) (neeche); \(z = 0\) ka koi argument nahi.
• Principal argument \(\arg z\) woh ek argument hai jo \((-\pi, \pi]\) mein ho.
• Pehle quadrant, phir \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}|b/a|\), phir table.

blocks.title: Aam ghaltiyan
blocks.text:
• Imaginary part ke liye \(r\cos\theta\) likh dena (yahi ghalti Example 12 mein chhapi hai). Imaginary part hamesha \(r\sin\theta\) hai.
• \(r\) ko negative le lena. Modulus \(r = |z|\) faasla hai, kabhi negative nahi.
• \(a < 0\) ho to bhi quadrant check kiye baghair calculator ka \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) likh dena.
• Principal argument range se bahar dena, jaise \(-\pi/3\) ki jagah \(5\pi/3\). Agar angle \(\pi\) se bara aa jaye to \(2\pi\) tafreeq kijiye.
• Calculator degree mode mein ho aur jawab radians mein chahiye (ya ulta). Jawab likhne se pehle mode check kijiye.
